title: Why Accuracy Beats Speed in KYC Data Entry
excerpt: Notes from a year of verifying financial records, and why small habits catch the discrepancies that matter most.
content: A year into banking KYC data entry, the lesson that stuck with me wasn't about typing speed — it was about the habits that catch a discrepancy before it becomes someone else's problem down the line.

Every document that crosses a compliance desk carries a small chance of being slightly wrong: a mismatched address, an expired ID, a signature that doesn't quite line up. Most of the job is building a rhythm where those small mismatches actually surface instead of sliding through.

The habit that helped most was treating every record like it would be audited the same day — not eventually, today. It sounds simple, but it changes how carefully you cross-check a field before moving to the next one.

None of this is glamorous work, but it's the kind of quiet reliability that compounds. A team that trusts its data doesn't have to double-check everything downstream, and that trust is built one careful entry at a time.

title: What Building AI Workflows Taught Me
excerpt: Turning ChatGPT, Claude, and Notion AI into an actual system instead of a pile of open tabs.
content: For a while, my "AI workflow" was just a dozen open tabs — ChatGPT for one thing, Claude for another, Notion AI half-finished somewhere in between. It worked, technically, but it wasn't a system.

The shift happened when I stopped treating each tool as a one-off assistant and started treating them as stages in a pipeline: research and brainstorming in one place, drafting and structuring in another, and a final review pass somewhere else entirely.

The biggest unlock was writing down the handoffs — what goes from step one into step two, and in what format. Once that was explicit, the whole thing stopped feeling like juggling and started feeling like an actual workflow.

It also changed how I learn new technical concepts. Instead of reading and hoping it sticks, I now use AI tools to quiz myself, summarize in my own words, and flag the parts I clearly don't understand yet — which turns out to be faster than it sounds.

title: From Data Entry to Web Dev: A Self-Taught Path
excerpt: How compliance work and late-night coding ended up teaching each other more than expected.
content: By day, I was verifying KYC documents. By night, I was slowly teaching myself HTML, CSS, and JavaScript — two completely different worlds that, it turns out, aren't as separate as they look.

Compliance work trains a specific kind of attention: check the field, check it again, notice when something is off even if you can't immediately explain why. That same instinct turned out to be exactly what debugging a broken layout or a silent JavaScript error requires.
Being self-taught meant a lot of trial and error — building a business website end to end, then a Discord bot, then a Chrome extension, each one teaching me something the last one didn't cover.

The throughline across both halves of my work is the same: accuracy first, speed second. Whether it's a mortgage record or a line of code, the version that's careful tends to age a lot better than the version that's fast.
